![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/2242cf493c6307d8c6f2dac778efe6f89ca4ba6f04203940076360613c8dc9b0.png)

A $13\,\text{ft}$ support pole leans against a vertical wall, forming an angle $\theta $ with the ground. The base of the pole $B$ is being pulled toward the wall at a rate of $2\,\text{ft/s}.$ At what rate is $\theta $ increasing at the moment when the top of the pole $T$ is $5\,\text{ft}$ above the ground? Do not round the answer.

The angle is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{rad/s}.$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14212968/assets/e08cddcde0d709ebe455b8d8935174955798b877f054dab0de74d06035accc91.png)

In the figure, $x$ is the horizontal distance from the base of the pole to the wall, $y$ is the vertical distance between the top of the pole and the ground, and $z$ is the length of the pole. The quantity $z=13$ feet does not change with time because the pole's length doesn't change.

We wish to calculate $\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}$ when $y=5$ feet. To do this, let's start by setting up a relation between $x$ and $z.$ Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $x$ and $z$ are the adjacent and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{z} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\frac{x}{13} \\ x & =13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate both sides of the equation with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(13\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given information, we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-2$ (negative because the horizontal distance is decreasing). Substituting this into the above, we reach

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =(-13\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{2}{13} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t} & =\frac{2}{13}\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Relative to the angle $\theta ,$ the sides $y$ and $z$ are the opposite and hypotenuse, respectively. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{y}{z} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\frac{5}{13} \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡\theta  & =\frac{13}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}\theta }{\text{d}t}=\frac{2}{13}\cdot \frac{13}{5}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

So, the angle is increasing at a rate of $\frac{2}{5}\,\text{rad/s}.$
